facts:
Contract states a right of substitution: True
Right is fettered: False
Who would pay a substitute: worker

Account of substitution in practice:
Twice this year the worker sent a qualified colleague of their own choosing without asking the client first, and paid the colleague directly. The client accepted the substitute's work without objection.
reference_answer: Fail. The worker has an unfettered right of substitution that has been genuinely exercised: they choose the substitute, pay them, and the client accepted the work. An unfettered right to send a substitute is inconsistent with a contract of service (Express & Echo Publications Ltd v Tanton; Staffordshire Sentinel Newspapers Ltd v Potter), so personal service is absent.

facts:
Who decides what work and what order: The depot supervisor allocates tasks at the start of each shift and moves the worker between stations during the day.
Who decides how work is performed: The worker follows the client's written operating procedures and is corrected on the spot where the method departs from them.
Who sets the hours and location: Shifts are 07:00 to 15:30 on a rota published by the client, worked entirely at the client's warehouse.
Report to a manager or not: The worker reports to the shift supervisor and is subject to the client's disciplinary procedure.
reference_answer: Pass. The client decides what work is done and in what order, dictates the method, fixes the hours and place, and supervises and disciplines the worker. That is control across what, how, when and where (Ready Mixed Concrete), well beyond the sufficient degree required.

facts:
Who decides what work and what order: The contractor agrees an outcome and a deadline, then plans the stages of work without reference to the client.
Who decides how work is performed: The contractor selects the technical method, materials and sequence, subject only to statutory standards.
Who sets the hours and location: There are no set hours. The contractor attends when they choose.
Report to a manager or not: There is no manager or reporting line.
reference_answer: Fail. The client only specifies the end result; the contractor decides how, when and where the work is done, and there is no reporting line. Control limited to specifying the result points away from employment, so the control condition is not satisfied.

facts:
Who decides what work and what order: The client sets the project priorities and can move the consultant between workstreams at short notice.
Who decides how work is performed: The consultant uses their own specialist judgement on technical method, which the client could not direct.
Who sets the hours and location: Core hours of 10:00 to 16:00 at the client's office.
Report to a manager or not: The consultant reports weekly to the client's programme manager.
reference_answer: Pass. Although the client cannot direct the specialist technique, it controls what work is done, when and where, and the consultant reports to its manager. Skilled professionals can still be under sufficient control (Cassidy v Ministry of Health; Beloff v Pressdram), so control is satisfied.

facts:
Who decides what work and what order: The owner has a contractual right to direct all work on the property, but in practice rarely gives instructions.
Who decides how work is performed: The caretakers organise the daily work themselves.
Who sets the hours and location: The caretakers live on site and are expected to be available, but set their own daily routine.
Report to a manager or not: There is no day-to-day supervision; the owner visits a few times a year.
reference_answer: Pass. The owner holds an overarching contractual right to direct the work. An ultimate right of control is sufficient even without day-to-day supervision (White v Troutbeck SA), and a right counts even where it is rarely or never exercised (Christa Ackroyd Media Ltd v HMRC).

facts:
Who decides what work and what order: The governing body appoints the official to matches and can stop offering appointments.
Who decides how work is performed: During matches the official makes independent decisions, but must follow the body's code of conduct and is assessed and given feedback after every match.
Who sets the hours and location: Match times and venues are set by the fixture list.
Report to a manager or not: The official is monitored by assessors and can be removed from the list for poor performance.
reference_answer: Pass. Control need not be exercisable during the work itself; a sufficient framework of control through codes of conduct, assessment and the sanction of removal from the list is enough (HMRC v Professional Game Match Officials Ltd). Independence of judgement during the match does not defeat it.

facts:

Who decides how work is performed: The presenter has considerable creative freedom in how they present, but the broadcaster holds contractual editorial control.
Who sets the hours and location: The broadcast schedule sets the hours; the presenter must be in the studio for each show.
Report to a manager or not: The presenter reports to the programme editor.
reference_answer: Pass. The broadcaster's contractual right to control content, format and scheduling is sufficient, even though the presenter has considerable creative freedom (Kickabout Productions Ltd v HMRC; Christa Ackroyd Media Ltd v HMRC).

reference_answer: Pass. Lawful authority to command, so far as there is scope for it, is enough; the engager need not direct the technique (Zuijs v Wirth Brothers). The client controls what, when and where and can require rework, so control is sufficient. For skilled work, the court also asks whose business it is (Lane v Shire Roofing).

reference_answer: Pass. Where a worker is lent to another party, the general employer keeps the authority to control how the work is done unless it clearly passes (Mersey Docks and Harbour Board v Coggins & Griffith). The general employer retains that authority, so control is present.

reference_answer: Fail. The client controls only the end result, and the security policy arises from site requirements rather than a general right to direct. Control carries less weight for a skilled worker with many clients (Hall v Lorimer), and here it is not sufficient.

facts:
Does defective work need correcting: Yes. The contractor must return and fix any defects at their own expense under a twelve-month warranty, with no further payment.
    Can they make a loss on engagement: Yes. Work is quoted at a fixed price, and the contractor absorbs any overruns in time or materials.
keywords: own time and at their own expense
reference_answer: Self employment, strong. The contractor must put right defective work at their own expense and prices work at a fixed price, absorbing overruns. Rectification at own cost and genuine loss-making risk both point strongly towards self-employment (Market Investigations; Hall v Lorimer).

facts:
Does defective work need correcting: Errors are corrected during paid hours at the client's cost.
    Can they make a loss on engagement: No. The worker is paid hourly and supplies nothing beyond personal safety boots.
reference_answer: Employment, strong. The worker is paid for time spent correcting errors and cannot make a loss, being paid by the hour with no costs. There is no entrepreneurial risk (Lee Ting Sang v Chung Chi-Keung), which points towards employment.

facts:
Does defective work need correcting: No obligation to correct work at own cost.
    Can they make a loss on engagement: No. Paid a day rate. The only risk is not being offered further days.
reference_answer: Employment, strong. The worker is paid a day rate and the only risk is not being offered work, which is not entrepreneurial risk (Lee Ting Sang). IR35 cases treat a day rate with no real risk of loss as carrying little financial risk.

facts:
Does defective work need correcting: Not applicable.
    Can they make a loss on engagement: Yes. The performer pays a fee to the venue each night before earning anything, negotiates their own prices with customers, and has ended nights out of pocket.
reference_answer: Self employment, strong. The individual pays fees to the venue that must be covered before any profit and bears the economic risk of a loss-making night (Stringfellow Restaurants Ltd v Quashie). That is genuine financial risk.

facts:
Does defective work need correcting: Yes, at the contractor's own cost.
    Can they make a loss on engagement: Yes. The contractor pays for materials, two employees and insurance, none of which is reimbursed, and has written off bad debts from clients who failed to pay.
reference_answer: Self employment, strong. The contractor bears significant unreimbursed costs, employs staff, and carries the risk of bad debts, as well as rectifying work at own cost. These are strong indicators of financial risk pointing towards self-employment (Hall v Lorimer; Market Investigations).

facts:

reference_answer: Employment, strong. Expenses are reimbursed and equipment is provided, so the worker bears no costs; reimbursed expenses are not financial risk. There is no rectification obligation and no possibility of loss.

facts:

reference_answer: Self employment, strong. The worker rectifies unsatisfactory work in their own time without pay, which HMRC's CEST tool treats as pointing to self-employment, and bears overruns on quoted work, a genuine risk of loss.

facts:

reference_answer: Employment, strong. The worker is paid for the time spent correcting errors and is paid by the hour regardless of results, so there is no risk of loss. Both point towards employment.

facts:

facts:

    Can they make a loss on engagement: No, I invoice a day rate.

facts:
Does defective work need correcting: Yes, I put right anything that isn't up to standard myself.
    Can they make a loss on engagement: I've lost money on a couple of jobs this year, where the price of materials went up after I'd already quoted.
reference_answer: Self employment, strong. The worker has actually made losses on fixed-price work when costs rose, and rectifies defects themselves. This is genuine loss-making risk, not merely earning less.

facts:

reference_answer: Employment, moderate. The risk-bearing terms are not reflected in practice: the client pays for fixes and the contractor is paid hourly. Risks that exist only on paper carry little weight (Autoclenz Ltd v Belcher), so the factor points towards employment.

facts:
Does defective work need correcting: No. Any poor work is dealt with by the site foreman.

reference_answer: Employment, strong. The self-employed label and gross invoicing are not conclusive; in substance the worker is paid by the hour and bears no risk (Ferguson v John Dawson & Partners; Young & Woods Ltd v West).

facts:

    Can they make a loss on engagement: Yes. Although the contract refers to a day rate, in practice each deliverable is quoted as a fixed fee, and the consultant absorbed a significant overrun on the last project.
reference_answer: Self employment, strong. In practice the consultant prices work on a fixed-fee basis, has absorbed an overrun, reworks rejected work unpaid, and carries professional indemnity insurance. The substance shows genuine financial risk despite the day-rate label.

facts:

    Can they make a loss on engagement: No. The contractor works through their own limited company on a day rate; the only risk is the client ending the contract.
reference_answer: Employment, strong. A contractor paid a day rate with no real risk of loss carries little financial risk, which weighed against the contractor in IR35 cases such as Dragonfly Consulting Ltd v HMRC. Working through a limited company does not change this.

facts:
Does defective work need correcting: No. Defects are dealt with by the company's own staff at the company's cost.

reference_answer: Employment, moderate. The plumber supplies a van and tools, but the engager fixes the rate, materials are recharged and defects are the company's cost. Some financial exposure is compatible with worker status where the individual is integrated and controlled (Pimlico Plumbers Ltd v Smith).

facts:

reference_answer: Employment, moderate. At this clinic the surgeon is paid per session and bears no costs or rectification risk. Running a business elsewhere does not automatically defeat worker status for a particular engagement (Hospital Medical Group Ltd v Westwood).

facts:
Does defective work need correcting: Not applicable; the work is live and cannot be redone.
    Can they make a loss on engagement: Yes. The freelancer works for around twenty production companies, bears their own office, accounting and insurance costs, and has suffered bad debts and cancelled engagements.
reference_answer: Self employment, strong. The freelancer bears their own business expenses and the risk of bad debts and cancelled engagements across many clients, and can make a profit or loss depending on how well they run the business (Hall v Lorimer). Financial risk does not require capital investment.
